Learning Objectives:

  1. Define metabolism

  2. Define catabolism and anabolism

  3. Classify pathways as either catabolic or anabolic

  4. Outline the value of irreversible steps within a metabolic pathway

  5. Explain the processes by which cells regulate metabolism

Introduction

What does metabolism mean to you? For most people, metabolism is associated with burning calories or breaking down ingested food. While this is the common use of the term metabolism, food digestion is only a part of our overall metabolism.

Metabolism, coming from the Greek word meaning ‘to change’, is ‘the sum of the chemical reactions that take place within each cell of a living organism and that provide energy for vital processes and for synthesizing new organic material” (https://www.britannica.com/science/metabolism).

There are more than a thousand individual chemical reactions taking place within even the smallest of organisms. Some of them are used to digest food or macromolecules, while others are used to build the molecules of life. Regardless of the purpose of the individual reaction, all of them contribute to the metabolism of that organism. Let’s take a closer look.

NOTE: This lesson is going to be short on videos and activities because it is introducing you to the concepts needed for future lessons. Everything we cover here, we will cover again with specific examples later on.

Types of Chemical Processes

• Metabolism

    Although there are thousands of individual chemical reactions, there are a set of standard chemical pathways – series of consecutive chemical reactions – that are commonly utilized by organisms to generate energy and smaller molecules and use those molecules and energy to build macromolecules and cellular components. These pathways are classified as either anabolic or catabolic.

  • Anabolism

    A pathway used to form bonds between small molecules to synthesize larger molecules, such as macromolecules and even cells, is known as an anabolic or biosynthetic process. These pathways consume energy. The combination of all the anabolic pathways within an organism is known as anabolism.

    HINT: I always remember this because of anabolic steroids. These are what athletes take to try to BUILD big muscles. So if you see anabolism, think body BUILDer.

  • Catabolism

    A pathway that involves the breakdown or digestion of larger molecules for the generation of fuel and molecular building materials is known as a catabolic process. This is most commonly accomplished through oxidation reactions. In the process of breaking bonds, energy is released. The combination of all the catabolic pathways within an organism is known as catabolism. The remainder of this module will focus on catabolism.

    HINT: I always remember catabolism because if you know anything about cats, you know they are destructive a**holes. So if you see cat, think of a CATastrophe.

Together, anabolism and catabolism make up the entirety of an organism’s metabolism. Many metabolic pathways are complimentary to each other; for each anabolic process that generates a given biomolecule, there is a respective catabolic process to break it down. The primary pathways involved in biomolecule metabolism are listed below. We will discuss each of them in detail in Modules 4-7.

HINT: Notice anything that says genesis or synthesis is for generation of molecules (anabolic) and anything that says lysis or oxidation is for breakdown of molecules (catabolic).

Inside Chemical Pathways

Chemical pathways, although made up of different steps or reactions, have a set of standards that apply to all of them. Let's talk about them.

  1. As you can see in the image at the opening of this lesson, the pathways are interconnected and interdependent.

    • Many pathways utilize the products from another pathway as their starting reactants.

    • Energy-releasing reactions are linked with energy-consuming reactions. These are called coupled reactions and will be discussed in lesson 2.

  2. The standard currency of energy is ATP, which we will discuss in lesson 2.

  3. There are a finite number of reaction types, meaning certain reactions are common in various pathways.

  4. The products of the individual steps of a process, those that will be generated and consumed within the pathway itself, are known as intermediates.

    • Just as there are common reactions within the pathways, there is a standard set of intermediates that are utilized by multiple metabolic pathways. We will discuss these in more detail in lesson 2.

  5. The reactions within the metabolic pathways are catalyzed by enzymes.

  6. While many reactions within a given pathway are reversible, meaning they can proceed in the forward or reverse direction, each pathway consists of one or more steps that are considered irreversible.

    • These are steps in which the thermodynamic cost of reversing the reaction is so great that, in a natural state, cells will not perform the reverse reaction.

    • We will discuss these further as we detail the steps of the major metabolic pathways in future modules.

    • These irreversible reactions are also called rate-limiting steps, and are valuable because they are often the reactions targeted for regulating the progression of the pathway, becoming the bottlenecks for the subsequent steps. Speaking of regulation…

  7. All metabolic pathways are tightly regulated via communication within and between cells. In general, metabolic pathways are controlled by the same 3 methods. Let’s check those out next!
Regulation of Metabolic Processes
Intro to regulation videoOpen on YouTube

Organisms are incredibly resilient. Unbeknownst to the lay person, inside of us, our bodies are constantly working and adapting to maintain a constant environment that keeps our organs, and overall life, operating. For example, we are able to maintain an internal temperature of approximately 98.6*F regardless of the temperature around us. This tendency “to maintain stability while adjusting to conditions that are optimal for survival” (https://www.britannica.com/science/homeostasis) is known as homeostasis.

When it comes to biochemistry and metabolism, our bodies are able to not only adapt to maintain a consistent environment regardless of external stressors (for example, our pupils dilate and constrict depending on the amount of available light), but they can also compartmentalize and maintain different consistent environments in different areas depending on the needs and functions of a given tissue/organ. This was first observed by Claude Bernardo, who noticed organisms adjust both quantitatively (in concentration of substances) and temporally (in different ways at different times).

Why would we need such tight regulations of our metabolic processes?

1. Different environments demand different metabolites and survival is dependent upon being able to always produce what is needed.

For example, a change in diet will change the nutrients that are being obtained through food. This could mean that something the body was previously synthesizing on its own is no longer necessary because it is being obtained within the food, or it could mean that a necessary nutrient is no longer supplied through diet, and therefore must be synthesized by our body in order to survive.

2. It would require a constant supply of food.

If the body immediately metabolized a meal to completion as soon as it was consumed, there would be no way to store the energy for later use.

3. Different tissues have different demands.

Your muscle tissues, including your heart, require a large amount of energy to function properly, which means the metabolism must be skewed in favor of catabolism in these parts of the body. Red blood cells, however, do not really require energy at all, as they are floating along in their very own lazy river; therefore, generating a large amount of ATP within the red blood cells would be a waste.

4. Many byproducts can be toxic.

Several pathways create products other than the final output. These are called byproducts. In some instances, these by products are harmful to cells, and so they need a way to manage them. For example, the Oxidative Phosphorylation (OxPhos) pathway (discussed in Lesson 4) is efficient at generating ATP, but in the process, it creates hydrogen peroxides, which are damaging to cells. The cells have developed mechanisms to neutralize these reactive oxygen species (ROS); however, in order to prevent cellular damage, the neutralization process must be able to keep up with their production. This would not be possible if OxPhos was running non-stop.

Now that we know why regulation is necessary, let’s look at the three ways in which cells regulate metabolism. These are: DNA level control, control of catalytic activities, and modification of substrate concentrations. As we previously mentioned, the chemical reactions that make up the steps in metabolic pathways are catalyzed by enzymes. As we mentioned in the last module, if you control the enzyme-substrate interaction, and specifically at the points of those non-reversible reactions, you can control the entire pathway. You will see that all 3 modes of regulation, all of which should look familiar to you, are focused on just that.

Three Ways to Regulate Metabolic Processes:

Enzyme Concentration

While the enzymes are not used up in the chemical reaction, they can become damaged or degrade over time. Cells are constantly synthesizing fresh enzymes to replace their degraded counterparts and maintain the efficiency of the catalyst. A cell will utilize molecular inducers or repressors to signal the cell to increase or decrease the synthesis of the enzyme on an as-needed basis. This is most often done at the DNA level, altering the rate of transcription of the genes that encode the enzymes. Furthermore, a cell can “turn on” the pathway to break down a target enzyme if it is present in excess of what is necessary at the moment.

Substrate Concentration

Instead of changing the concentration of the enzyme, a cell can also adjust the available concentration of the substrate the enzyme acts on. This is most frequently accomplished by compartmentalizing pathways within cells away from the substrate. Therefore, the substrate must be shuttled into the area where the enzyme is present/the pathway takes place before it can trigger the cascade of reactions.

This of this like food moving from your stomach through your intestines. Your body begins digestion in the stomach, and the only allows a small amount of food to enter into the intestine at a time, which is why you remain full for hours after completing a meal. This time-released food digestion optimizies the process, ensuring the most efficient nutrient absorption possible.

Catalytic Activity

The final metabolic control is to regulate the physical bonding of the enzyme and the substrate by altering the enzyme availability. This is done within a cell by one of two mechanisms: 1. Feedback inhibition where an excess of product from a pathway will bind to the enzyme and block its availability to the substrate. 2. Hormones will trigger the alteration of an enzyme activation site, therefore controlling the availability of the enzyme to the target substrate. This allows for tissue-specific regulation of metabolism.

Learning Objectives:

  1. Outline the thermodynamic mechanism of coupled reactions
  2. Define an activated carrier
  3. Identify the characteristics that make a molecule a good activated carrier
  4. Explain the characteristics of ATP that make it an energy-rich molecule

  6. Explain the importance of vitamin B in metabolism

Introduction

Remember from Module 2 that a reaction can only take place spontaneously if change in free energy is negative. As previously discussed, a pathway is a series of sequential reactions. For sequential reactions, change in free energy is additive. Therefore, a pathway will take place spontaneously if the sum of the free-energy change for the entire system is negative because the thermodynamically unfavorable reactions in the pathway can be driven by thermodynamically favorable reactions to which they are coupled.

Let's take a look at a simple two step pathway in which A is utimately converted to the products C and D, and B is an intermediate within the pathway.

Click on the two hotspots in the image to learn more.

• Step One: A --> B + C

    The first step, A--> B + C is not thermodynamically favorable (endergonic) and therefore would not happen spontaneously.

  • Step Two: B --> D

    However, the next step B-->D is so thermodynamically favorable (exergonic) that it will pull the pathway along, ultimately driving the production of B from A.
These two reactions are coupled by the shared intermediate B. Despite the energetically unfavorable initial step, this pathway will proceed spontaneously because the overall ΔG°ʹ is negative.

Activated Carriers

While reaction coupling is great for driving pathways, what if the goal is merely to convert X to Y, and not run an entire pathway? In this case, we still couple exergonic and endergonic reactions, but via a molecule that temporarily stores the energy from the exergonic reaction until it is needed for the endergonic reaction. These molecules are called activated carriers.

Activated carriers are small organic molecules that contain energy in a readily transferable form, most commonly as one or more functional groups or electrons. These molecules are able to diffuse rapidly and carry their bond energy from the site of energy generation to the site of biosynthesis.

Reactions can be coupled together with an activated carrier because it creates a shared intermediate. In this case, the overall free-energy change is the sum of the individual changes.

For this reason, combining the hydrolysis of an activated carrier molecule with a thermodynamically unfavorable reaction allows the progression of the unfavorable reaction.

We will discuss more about this process later in this lesson.

Properties of Activated Carriers

In order for a molecule to be a good energy carrier, it must be kinetically stable, but thermodynamically unstable.

  • Kinetic stability refers to the spontaneous reactivity, or rate of reaction of the molecule. Activated carriers are slow to react, and therefore will not degrade or participate in chemical reactions, without the presence of a catalyst.

  • Thermodynamic stability refers to spontaneity of the reaction. A thermodynamically unstable reaction is one that will occur spontaneously.

The combination of kinetic stability and thermodynamic instability means that the hydrolysis reactions of activated carrier will happen spontaneously, but will take a very long time without the presence of the appropriate enzyme. This is imperative for an energy carrier because it means they will release energy when they react while enabling enzymes to control the flow of free energy through the body (which means your cells can regulate the flow of free energy as needed because it can control enzymatic activity).

An example of a thermodynamically unstable, but kinetically stable reaction would be the conversion of coal to diamonds. This process happens naturally, but in the absence of extreme heat and pressure (catalysts), it happens very slowly.

The most important and versatile activated carrier in cells is adenosine 5’-triphosphate, more commonly known as ATP. Let’s dive into the properties of ATP that make it such a valuable molecule.

Adenosine Triphosphate

Here is the video from the last lesson. I told you it would be important for this lesson. This time, I want you to watch starting from 2:15 on.
ATPOpen on YouTube

ATP serves as the primary energy currency within cells. Most of catabolism involves extracting energy from fuels, carbohydrates and fats, and converting that energy into ATP (We will detail this process in the subsequent lessons). In return, ATP acts as the free-energy donor in most energy-requiring processes, including motion, active transport, and biosynthesis (anabolism).

The energetic value of ATP lies within the bonds that form this molecule. ATP is a nucleotide. Recall from module 1, lesson 1 that nucleotides are a 5-carbon sugar attached to a heterocyclic ring and at least one phosphate group. In the case of ATP, the sugar is ribose, the heterocyclic ring is adenine and, as the name suggests, there are three phosphate groups. The outer phosphates are adjoined to the molecule via dehydration synthesis, forming phosphoanhydride bonds.

It is in these phosphate groups, and specifically their phosphoanhydride bonds, that the free energy is stored, which is why ATP is often called a high-energy phosphate compound. a “squiggle” (~P) is often used to indicate high energy phosphoanhydride bonds, or bonds that release large amounts of free energy when hydrolyzed.

A large amount of free energy is liberated when ATP is hydrolyzed to adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and orthophosphate (Pi) or when ATP is hydrolyzed to adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and pyrophosphate (PPi):

The ATP-ADP Cycle

As shown in the Coupled Reactions image above (under activated carriers section), a thermodynamically unfavorable reaction sequence can be converted into a favorable one by coupling it to the hydrolysis of ATP molecules in a new reaction. In turn, ATP is formed from ADP and Pi when fuel molecules are oxidized; because this condensation reaction is energetically unfavorable, it must be coupled to a highly energetically favorable reaction to occur.

This ATP-ADP cycle is the fundamental mode of energy exchange in biological systems.
Phosphoryl-Transfer Potential

The final aspect of ATP that makes it such a valuable energy carrier lies in its phosphoryl-transfer potential, or the likelihood of ATP pulling a phosphate group from a different molecule vs. the likelihood of ATP having a phosphate group stripped by another molecule. The figure above shows the phosphoryl-transfer potential of common phosphorylated molecules in relation to ATP. As you can see, ATP has an intermediate phosphoryl-transfer potential, which is why ATP is able to function efficiently as a carrier of high energy phosphoryl groups. ADP will pick up Pi from those with higher transfer potential, forming ATP. It will release a phosphate to those with a lower potential, which happens to coincide with those molecules that are lower in energy.

Additional Activated Carriers

While ATP is the most common activated carrier, it is far from the only one utilized repeatedly. As we proceed through our metabolic pathways, you will see there are several other key molecules for energy transfer.

Here are a few of the ones we will highlight as we continue throughout the semester:

CoEnzyme A

Our next lesson will open with Acetyl CoA, a molecule of Coezyme A linked to an acyl group via a high-energy thioester bond. The transfer of this acyl group is important in the breakdown of fatty acids and the synthesis of other lipids.

Biotin

Biotin is a vitamin that is used by a number of enzymes to transfer a carboxyl group to a substrate. This is an essential step in the formation of Oxaloacetate, the beginning molecule of the Citric Acid Cycle (lesson 3).

Tetrahydrofolate (THF)

THF donates one-carbon units to molecules during the synthesis of amino acids and nucleic acids. This is especially important during fetal development where it contributes to neural tube formation, which is why pregnant women are encouraged to take folic acid supplements. Supplemental folic acid is known to prevent up to 70% of neural tube defects. Interestingly, the formation of THF from folate depends upon another activated carrier, NADPH.

You are going to see THF come into play in the formation of several biomolecules, so pay attention as we go through modules 5-7 and look for it!

S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM)

SAM is a common methyl-transfer intermediate. One of the most common uses for methyl transfer is to regulate gene expression; however, SAM is known to transfer methyl groups to and from nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids.

Electron Carriers

Another type of coupled reactions are Reduction-Oxidation, or redox, reactions, which involve the transfer of a high-energy electron from one molecule to another. Redox reactions are valuable ways to transfer energy through cells, as you can see in the image below. We will explore their role in biosynthesis, where NADP+ is converted to NADPH to act as a reducing agent for anabolic reactions , as well as the oxidation of fuel, in which NAD+, FAD+, and FMN+ are reduced to NADH, FADH2, and FMNH2 and used to transfer electrons that will be used to drive the production of ATP. If you listened closely, you heared some of these molecules mentioned in the activated carriers video. Lesson 3 will focus on the production of ATP, including the role of these oxidizing agents.

Introduction

Ok, so by now, you should understand what metabolism is, and that we need to breakdown the foods we eat into their components for two reasons: 1. we need the parts (monomers) so we can build other macromolecules that we need and 2. we need the energy that comes from breaking the bonds to run, well, everything.

As we discussed in the previous lesson, most of that energy is going to be stored in some form of active carrier, likely ATP, so we can shuttle it around and use it as needed. Therefore, as we breakdown our food, a process known as oxidation, if you recall, we do it in a stepwise manner controlled by enzymes instead of in a single burning step. Preparing for Catabolism

Food molecules are broken down in three stages.

Explore the three hotspots in the image below to learn about them.

• Stage 1

    Digestion and Absorption. Large food molecules are broken down into simple subunits. This is also known as dietary digestion.

  • Stage 2

    Primary Catabolism. Simple subunits are broken down into acetyl CoA. Limited amounts of ATP and NADH are produced.

  • Stage 3

    Cellular Respiration. Complete oxidation of the acetyl group in acetyl CoA to water and carbon dioxide. Large amounts of ATP produced.

In subsequent modules, we will focus on step 2 as we explore the metabolism of individual biomolecules, but for now, let's talk about where they all converge: Step 3, Cellular Respiration.

Cellular respiration is our primary energy generation pathway. It is actually two pathways-the Citric Acid Cycle, the topic of the interest for this lesson, and Oxidative Phosphorylation, to be covered in the next lesson.

NOTE: Take a second look at the image above. Do you see the rectangle drawn around stages 2 and 3 with the word "mitochondrion" inside of it? Yep, that's right. Cellular respiration occurs within the mitochondrial matrix, which is why you have been told your entire life that the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.

As you can see from the image above, with minor exceptions that will be addressed later, all roads of catabolism lead to Acetyl CoA, so let us begin our energy generating journey there.
Acetyl Co-A

Coenzyme A is the activated carrier for acyl groups. When bound to an acyl group, Coenzyme A becomes Acetyl Coenzyme A, more commonly known as Acetyl CoA. The acetyl unit is a two carbon unit, and serves as the starting material for the citric acid cycle.

As we mentioned, Acetyl CoA is the merging point for most of catabolism. That is, various different biomolecules donate an acyl group to Coenzyme A. Pathways That Generate Acetyl CoA

How'd you do on that one? Did you get tripped up because the video only talked about carbohydrates/pyruvate and fatty acids? Well, if you recall, the image at the start of the lesson also showed amino acids. We will ultimately learn about three pathways that generate Acetyl CoA.

  1. Pyruvate Dehydrogenase. Glycolysis results in pyruvate molecules that then undergo oxidative decarboxylation.
  2. Degradation of Fatty Acids. Long fatty acid chains get broken down through beta oxidation.
  3. Amino Acid Degradation. The amino acids isoleucine, leucine, threonine, lysine, and tryptophan directly generate Acetyl CoA during oxidation. Other amino acids are broken down into pyruvate, which is then oxidized into Acetyl CoA.

Why Does Acetyl CoA Matter?

Why do you think all roads lead to Acetyl CoA? Typically, when there is a single focal point such as Acetyl CoA, it is not by accident. This is for regulatory purposes. As we mentioned, all of this is happening in the mitochondria. The compartmentalization of Coenzyme A in the mitochondrial matrix allows for control of metabolism. The formation of Acetyl CoA is decisive and irreversible. While we will learn that Acetyl CoA can be utilized for more than the citric acid cycle, once formed, there are only a limited number of options for what must happen next. Therefore our bodies only generate Acetyl Co-A when necessary by moving molecules into the mitochondria from the cytosol.

The Citric Acid Cycle

The Citric Acid Cycle, also know as the Kreb's Cycle (my preference, but for this course I will use Citric Acid Cycle because that is what the book uses) or the Tricarboxylic Acid Cycle, is a sequence of eight reactions that oxidizes the acetyl group of acetyl-CoA into carbon dioxide. In this process, it will reduce additional activated carriers that we will then utilize in the next lesson, the electron transport chain, to generate ATP.

Sidenote: We will learn in future modules that the citric acid cycle is also important for gluconeogenesis, lipogenesis, and the interconversion of amino acids, meaning it is also important for anabolism, not just catabolism, but for now, all we are focusing on is catabolism.

FUN FACT: Most of these processes occur in most of our tissues, but the liver is the only tissue where they all occur to a significant extent. Therefore, the repurcussions are huge when there is a large breakdown of liver tissue. Love your liver because it is vital for energy formation!

Let's start with the nuts and bolts of the cycle, and then we will dig into the nitty gritty details:

What Goes IN?

  • We already talked about how we always start with Acetyl CoA. While this is going to bind to another molecule (oxaloacetate), we are going to regenerate the material it binds to (thus creating a circle), so it is not going on our input list.
  • We will also need H2O. Remember, water is great for breaking down molecules in a process known as hydrolysis. As a whole process, cellular respiration actually generates water, but this part consumes it.
  • NAD+ and FAD, as these are going to become our activated carriers.
  • ADP. We will get to produce some ATP in the cycle.

What Comes OUT?

  • CO2. We are going to create two carbon dioxide per turn of the cycle.
  • NADH and FADH2. Our activated carriers transporting high energy electrons for the next steps! Each turn of the cycle creates three NADH and one FADH2.*
  • A single ATP is produced with each turn of the cycle. This is indirect and comes from the formation of GTP, but you just need to know you get one ATP per cycle.

*THIS is the primary reason for the citric acid cycle. This is what it's all about. We aren't getting much ATP direct from the cycle, but we are transferring lots of energy in the form of electrons (really, protons), so we can run the electron transport chain to make tons of ATP later.

The net reaction of the citric acid cycle is: Acetyl CoA + 3NAD+ + FAD + ADP + 2H2O --> 2CO2 + 3NADH + FADH2 + ATP + 2H+ + CoA.

As you saw in the video, the citric acid cycle can be broken down into two major sections, which can essentially be described as the start of the cycle and then the regeneration of the starting material in order to prepare for future cycles.

REMINDER: Many pathways have bottlenecks or rate-limiting steps, and these are the ones that will control the pathways. The citric acid cycle is broken down into two sections, but these are not the same as the rate-limiting or regulatory steps. In each section, we are going to discuss the regulatory steps separately. I do not want you to confuse the two sections from the regulatory and rate-limiting steps.
Steps One-Four

The Citric Acid Cycle begins with step one binding of the acetyl moeity of acetyl-CoA, a two carbon molecule, to oxaolacetate, a four cabon molecule, to form a six carbon citrate. This reaction is catalyzed by citrate synthase.

ENZYME REMINDER: A synthase is an enzyme that catalyzes a synthesis, or molecule forming, reaction in which two units are joined usually without the direct participation of ATP.

The resulting six carbon molecule is then metabolized into a four carbon molecule. Each time a carbon is lost from the main molecule is a vital step you need to know.

The first time happens in step three. At this point, citrate has been converted into isocitrate. Isocitrate is converted to α-Ketogluterate via the enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase. This process will release a carbon in the form of carbon dioxide. In addition to the formation of CO2, we will reduce NAD+ to NADH.

ENZYME REMINDER: A dehydrogenase in an enzyme that will create an electron carrying molecule, such as NADH or FADH2.

Notice that this is technically a two step reaction? That is because there is an unstable intermediate, oxalosuccinate, that is formed first. It is an α-ketoacid that binds to the enzyme and is the one that actually loses the carbon dioxide molecule. You don't need to know the intermediate, but I wanted you to know what was going on there.

The very next step of the cycle, step four, the second carbon is removed. The five carbon α-Ketogluterate is converted into four carbon Succinyl-CoA via α-Ketogluterate dehydrogenase complex. Once again, NAD+ is reduced to NADH and CO2 is formed.

ENZYME REMINDER: Anytime you see "complex" at the end of the enzyme name, it is because this is actually more than one enzyme operating as a unit.

FUN FACT: Isotope-labeling studies revealed that the two carbon atoms that enter each cycle are not the ones that leave. The two carbon atoms that enter the cycle as the acetyl group are retained in the initial two decarboxylation reactions and then remain incorporated in the four-carbon acids of the cycle while two different carbon atoms are released.
Steps Five-Eight

The second stage of the citric acid cycle is a series of steps to regenerate oxaloacetate in order to prepare for subsequent turns of the cycle.

Along the way, we produce ATP, FADH2, and another NADH.

The step I would like you to know in this half of the cycle is step six where we convert succinate to fumarate by transfering two hydrogen atoms from succinate to FAD to create FADH2.

This is completed with the help of the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase. We are going to see succinate dehydrogenase pop up again in the next lesson, which is the primary reason I wanted to point it out to you.

Can you guess why I highlighted the other reactions? If you guessed it is because they are places the citric acid cycle is regulated, you would be correct!

But, before we move on to regulation, I better check to make sure you followed everything up until now...

Regulation of The Citric Acid Cycle

So, as I mentioned, there are three main reactions I wanted you to know from the citric acid cycle because they are the primary regulatory steps. Let's check out this video and see what they say about them.
Regulation and InhibitionOpen on YouTube

Did you catch all three? And then we can't forget the first way we talked about for cycle regulation, meaning we have four primary ways we regulate the cycle:

1. We already discussed how one way we regulate the cycle is through compartmentalization/formation of Acetyl-CoA. If we don't create Acetyl-CoA within the mitochondria, we don't have the materials we need to begin the cycle. The formation of Acetyl Co-A is decisive and irreversible. Once we create it, it has to go somewhere. While that somewhere doesn't HAVE to be the citric acid cycle, it usually is. The formation of Acetyl Co-A is inhibited by high levels of ATP, NADH, and Acetyl Co-A itself.

2. As mentioned in the video, the enzyme citrate synthase is regulated through feed back inhibition. The product, Citrate, of the first reaction Acetyl CoA + Oxaloacetate --> Citrate will inhibit the reaction itself, therefore stopping the cycle. Citrate synthase will also be inhibited by high levels of ATP, which makes sense given that the main goal of the cycle is to generate products that will lead to ATP formation.

3. and 4. I want to talk about the next two together. Notice anything similar about the enzymes that catalyze the two additionaly regulatory steps I pointed out (actual steps 3 and 4)? Or perhaps about the two reactions themselves? Well, they are both run by dehydrogenases (isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase), and both require the availability of the activated carrier NAD+.

  • NAD+ contains the cofactor Niacin (that's a vitamin)
  • Thiamin (that's a vitamin too) is also a coenzyme for α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex

    • What I'm saying is, TAKE YOUR VITAMINS

  • Isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex are activated by calcium. Can you think of times this might be important for a cycle that leads to energy production? I can... Muscle contraction! When your muscles contract, calcium levels go up, so these dehydrogenases are kicked on, kicking the cycle into high gear to produce more ATP to keep those muscles running.

  • On the other side of this, in the absence of free NAD+ to accept hydrogens, the cycle will slow down because it is presumed that ATP is not needed.

FUN FACT: There are other dehydrogenases in the citric acid cycle; we talked about succinate dehydrogenase, and then there is malate dehyrodrogenase that rounds out the cycle in the final step. However, these are not the primary regulatory steps of the cycle. Succinate dehydrogenase is regulated by the concentration of oxaloacetate, which is regulated by malate dehydrogenase. Studies have shown that the availability of oxaloacetate is determined mostly by the rest of the cycle-it seems your body will regenerate oxaloacetate pretty readily when it uses it up.
Other Cycle Distruptions

One final note is that the inhibitions mentioned above are all natural regulations of the citric acid cycle. This is different from inhibitions that are not regulatory. Several poisons and deficiencies will block the cycle, resulting in insuffiencent energy formation.

Fluoroacetate

Fluoroacetate is a poison found in plants (none native to North America) that is toxic when ingested. It is especially dangerous to grazing animals. As you can see from the image above, it inhibits the conversion of Citrate to Isocitrate. It is used as an industrial pesticide and anticancer agent. In the US, it is used to kill coyotes, although use has been severly restricted by the EPA since 1972.

Malonate

Malonate is another poison that closely resembles succinate. It can be found in legumes. It acts as a competitive inhibitor for succinate dehydrogenase, causing the accumulation of succinate. Using malonate on muscle cells is actually part of the process of how Hans Krebs discovered the steps to the Kreb's cycle, and that it was indeed a cycle.

Arsenite and Hyperammonemia

Arsenite, the most toxic form of aresenic poison will inhibit the cycle by blocking α-ketogluatarate dehydrogenase complex.

High concentrations of ammonia can also inhibit the enzyme. Advanced liver disease and several genetic diseases (to be discussed later) result in hyperammonemia, a condition that leads to excess ammonia production. The end result is loss of consciousness, coma and convulsions, and often death.

What Goes IN?

-NADH and FADH2. Specifically, the electrons from these activated carriers, and the energy they carry. More on this next.

-ADP. The whole purpose here is phosphorylation of ADP to make ATP, so we need ADP to phosphorylate.

-Oxygen. This is an oxidative phosphorylation and the reason we need to breathe. Oxygen is going to be our final electron acceptor.

What Comes OUT?

- Water. When oxygen combines with the final electron, it will form water.

-NAD+ and FAD. We are going to remove the high enery electrons (and protons-more on this soon) and regenerate our carriers so we can return them to the citric acid cycle to keep the shuttle running.

-Lots and lots of ATP. That's the name of the game.

NOTE: In general, we are going to be able to create ~2.5 ATP per NADH and ~1.5 ATP per FADH2. This number is not exact for several reasons we will discuss later on, but is a decent estimate. Which means, from one turn of the citric acid cycle, we will be able to make 9 ATP, plus the one we made during the cycle is 10. Let's keep this number in mind as we move forward and consider how much energy we can yield from an entire catabolic pathway (remember, we started in the middle).

Now that we know what we are putting in and getting out, let's look at how it all comes together.
OxPhos Overview

Just like the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation can be summarized in two major steps:

1. The Electron Transport Chain where we are going to harvest the energy from those electrons we brough over. We are actually going to use this energy to move protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane to create a proton gradient.

2. ATP synthesis where we use the the proton gradient we generated to run a motor in a process called chemiosmosis or proton motive force. As the protons come back across the membrane, they drive the ATP synthase, forming ATP along the way.

The Electron Transport Chain consists of four protein complexes, each with a higher (hint: higher or lower) affinity for electrons than the one before. As electrons are are passed along the complexes, protons are pumped across the inner membrane to create a proton gradient. This gradient will be used to run the final step of OxPhos, ATP synthase. Did you get all that? If you did, you are an OxPhos overview rockstar! Just in case you did not, let's go over it again one more time, but let's start to add in a few more details.
Step One-Electron Transport Chain

The electron transport chain consists of the first four (of five) protein complexes. Let's highlight what's happening in these complexes

REMEMBER: A protein complex is a group of proteins that work together as a single unit

  • Delivery of electrons by NADH and FADH2. The electron transport chain obviously needs electrons. These are coming from the carriers we actived in the citric acid cycle. NADH will drop electrons into Complex I and FADH2 will drop them into Complex II (more on this soon). Once they drop electrons, they will go back to the citric acid cycle to pick up more.

  • Electron transfer and redox reactions. Electrons will be passed from complex to complex in a series of redox reactions. This is possible because each complex has a higher affinity for the electrons than the last, therefore they are able to pull the electrons along the chain. As they are passed, they slowly release energy, as seen in the image above.

  • Formation of a proton gradient. As electrons as passed, protons are simultaneously pumped acrossed the membrane into the intermembrane space. They cannot freely pass through the membrane, and must pass through the complexes. This is the value in the electron passing, as it allows for the build up of a proton gradient, where there are more protons in the intermembrane space than in the mitochondrial matrix. *This gradient will be used in the next step.

  • Splitting of oxygen to form water. At the end of the electron transport chain, electrons are transferred to molecular oxygen, which splits in half and takes up H+ to form water. So, we consume oxygen and form water during respiration.

*Location is important. Where does all of this take place again? Within the mitochondrial matrix, remember? The mitochondria has two membranes with a space between them. The protein complexes of OxPhos are actually embedded within the inner membrane itself. The protons can be pumped into the space in between to create this gradient. This has to happen in a place that a gradient can be created and controlled. Check out the image below for a review of where all the different reactions take place. For now, just remember, citric acid cycle was in the mitochondrial matrix, and now we are on the inner membrane and shuttling across it.

FUN FACT: Prokaryotic cells don't have mitochondria, but they can still perform cellular respiration. They pump protons across their cellular membrane and produce a chemiosmotic gradient there to drive ATP production.

Step Two-ATP Synthesis

The second step of OxPhos harnesses the power of the proton gradient generated by the electron transport chain to run the ATP synthase complex, also referred to as protein complex V (complex five) of OxPhos. You can see the gradient in the image above.

  • The protons (hydrogen ions) fall back down their chemiosmotic gradient through the enzyme ATP synthase.
  • This process is known as chemiosmosis.
    • Remember osmosis? The movement of water down a concentration gradient? It is the same thing, only now we are moving ions instead of water.
  • The flow of these protons physically turns the motor of the ATP synthase, which drives the generation of ATP.
  • Another term for this is proton-motive force.

OxPhos Complexes and Details

Ok, now that we understand what is going on in OxPhos, I want to talk a bit about the details of the complexes and how they work. This draw with me video is fantastic, so let's start here, and then we let's cover them together.
OxPhos StepsOpen on YouTube

Complex I - NADH Dehydrogenase

QUICK: Tell me what a dehydrogenase does. So, what is happening to NADH in this complex?

This is the entrypoint of NADH. NADH will be oxidized to NAD+. Each NADH will donate 2 electrons to the ETC. The path of an electron from NADH is as follows:

Complex I --> Coenzyme Q (AKA ubiquinone) --> Complex III --> Cytochrome C --> Complex IV --> oxygen

NOTICE: We bypassed Complex II. Complex II is not sequential to Complex I. It is a second entry point to the eletron transport chain.

Complex I pumps 4 protons across the inner membrane.

Complex II - Succinate Dehydrogenase

REMIND ME: Do you remember where we heard about succinate dehydrogenase before? That's right! It's actually a part of the citric acid cycle that also happens to be a second entry point for the ETC as well.

This is the entrypoint of FADH2. FADH2 will be oxidized to FAD. Each FADH2 will donate 2 electrons to the ETC. The path of an electron from FADH2 is as follows:

Complex II --> Coenzyme Q (AKA ubiquinone) --> Complex III --> Cytochrome C --> Complex IV --> oxygen

As you can see from the video, Complex II sit on the surface of the inner membrane. It is not a transmembrane protein complex, and therefore cannot pump protons across the inner membrane. Complex II pumps zero protons into the intermembrane space.

Complex III and IV- Cytochrome C Reductase and Oxidase

Electrons are passed from Complex I and II to a coenzyme that then passes them to Cytochrome C. The coenzymes and cytochromes are valuable mobile carriers that can move the electrons between the stationary protein complexes. Complex III will reduce the cytochrome C (transfer the electrons to cytochrome C), and then Complex IV will oxidize it, transferring the electrons from cytochrome C to oxygen.

Complex III pumps four protons across the membrane

Complex IV pumps three protons across the membrane

If you are keeping count, from complex I, that's 4+4+3=11 protons and from complex II, that 4+3=7 protons

Complex V - ATP Synthase

As mentioned, as the protons pump back through the ATP synthase, it works just like water moving a water wheel, which generates energy. In this case, that energy is ATP. For every four protons we can pump through ATP synthase, we will generate a single ATP molecule.

NOTE: Four protons : One ATP is a debated number. As you saw in the first video, they said 3:1. We are going with 4:1 for a few reasons, but the simplest to explain is that is what your book says, and that is what I am saying, so that is what you need to know.

If you are keeping count, that was 11 protons from an NADH entering complex I and 7 protons from an FADH2 entering complex II, which means 11/4= 2.75 ATP per NADH and 7/4=1.75 ATP per FADH2. With proton leakage explained below, we adjust to approximately 2.5 and 1.5 ATP respectively.

Regulation

The last thing we need to talk about is regulation of the pathway. Let's start with standard regulation, and then we will get into drugs and poisons.

Uncouplers

Energy comes in different forms. If you think about different environments and diets, not everyone needs the same types of energy. For example, someone living in Alaska with a diet high in easy-to-digest fish needs more heat energy than someone living in Africa with a diet high in tough-to-digest protein, who need less heat and more ATP to help with catabolic processes. The primary way our bodies regulate our energy formation is through regulation of oxidative phosphorylation, which makes sense considering this is our primary energy-generating pathway. For this reason, I really only want to focus on a single natural regulatory process for OxPhos: uncoupling.

In order to understand uncoupling, we need to take a quick step back and discuss coupling. In general, oxidation and phosphorylation are tightly coupled; oxidation via the ETC (step 1 of OxPhos) doesn't normally proceed without ADP being converted to ATP (step 2 of OxPhos). We pass electrons through the ETC, that passes protons into the intermembrane space which creates a proton gradient to drive ATP synthase. Eveything we just learned, right? Well, that's now always the case.

Sometimes, oxidation and phosphorylation become uncoupled (we do step one, but not step 2). The electron transport chain goes on as we discussed. Electrons passed, protons pumped. Oxidation is occuring. But, we do not create ATP. Instead, protons leak back through the membrane via uncoupling channels. This eliminates the proton gradient, meaning no more chemiosmosis/proton motive force, and no more ATP generation. Instead of ATP, the body makes heat. So, our bodies can use uncouplers to regulate temperature, shifting to heat energy production instead of ATP energy production when needed. We have an enzyme called thermogenin (AKA uncoupling protein-1) in our brown adipose tissue. This is the tissue that helps regulate our core temperature to keep our organs running if we are exposed to cold temperatures for too long.

FOOD FOR THOUGHT: Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a chemical that acts as an uncoupling agent, making the inner mitochondrial membrane leaky to protons. It was used until 1938 as a weight-loss drug.

Poisons and Diseases

Let's round things off by touching on a few drugs and diseases that impact OxPhos. There are dozens upon dozens, so I am just going to pick a few. The image I have selected is not specific to the ones I am selecting. I just wanted you to see that all complexes can be impacted.

NOTE: Be sure you understand the impact on OxPhos if we inhibit a Complex, not just if we give this drug, this complex will shut down. What happens if we shut down that complex?

Barbiturates

Ever see Valley of the Dolls? Probably not because it's from 1967. But, it's about a bunch of people that get addicted to Barbiturates. Barbiturates are "downer" pills. They often induce sleep, but are known to help cause feelings of relaxation. A common barbiturate is Amobarbitol.

Well, they inhibit Complex I of ETC/OxPhos. Tell me, if Complex I is inhibited, what happens? We can still make ATP, right? How? If we can still make ATP, why do you think inhibition of Complex I can be a problem, a fatal one?

Think about it. Complex II may be a second entry point, but it is not as efficient as Complex I, and is it certainly not as efficient as the combination of Complex I and II.

Rotenone, a compound found in rat poison and herbicide can also inhibit this complex, but I really want you to know the Barbiturates.

A number of genetic diseases impact complex I as well. Complex I is the most common complex to suffer from genetic disorders. Several mutations can lead to mitochondrial complex I deficiency, given that complex I is a complex of 44 different proteins. The degrees of deficiency can vary from a leaky membrane (causing inefficiency due to slight uncoupling) that would result in late onset diseases due to premature mitochondrial decay to fatal lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy due to a completely defective complex I.

Malonate

You should know this one already because we discussed it in the last lesson. Malonate inhibits Complex II, which, as we mentioned, is technically part of the citric acid cycle. This means that we cannot harvest the electrons from FADH2, and we could shut down the citric acid cycle, which will shut everything down!

Carbon Monoxide and Cyanide

Carbon Monoxide is dangerous for several reasons. It is a competitive inhibitor of oxygen of hemoglobin, so even though oxygen is present in the air, you can suffocate because you cannot circulate it through your body. However, both carbon monoxide and hemoglobin will inhibit complex IV.

What do you think happens if we shut down complex IV? What happens at the end of complex IV? Oxygen will accept the final electron, right. If you don't accept that final electron, it will sit with cytochrome c, which means cytochrome C is not available to accept another electron, and so on and so forth. The entire system backs up. We are once again shutting down the entire system here!
